decisions.evidence: Round 4 maker: enter a web address and click “Save bookmark.” Round 4 client: “When I saved https://example.com with the title ‘Example’, it showed up fine.”
decisions.note: Prototype review: saving a bookmark from a URL conforms to the reference.

decisions.evidence: Round 4 prototype used the address as the name when title was blank. Client: “I’d really expect the app to go grab the actual name of the page for me.”
decisions.note: Prototype review: the client replaced the incorrect URL-as-title fallback with automatic page-title collection.

decisions.evidence: Round 4 client, responding to the save prototype: “Ideally when I paste a link, it fills in the real title (and ideally a short description and the little site icon) on its own.”
decisions.note: Prototype review: the client requested missing automatic description and favicon collection.

decisions.evidence: Round 4 save-flow presentation and response discuss title, description, and site icon, but neither includes the required preview image; the client otherwise says, “The rest of what you showed me is what I want.”
decisions.note: Prototype review: automatic preview-image collection was absent and not surfaced by the client.

decisions.evidence: Round 4 client, after reviewing the initial save flow: “If I try to save a link I’ve already saved, I don’t want a second copy… recognize it and just take me to the one I already have so I can edit it.”
decisions.note: Prototype review: the client requested duplicate-save convergence missing from the presented flow.

decisions.evidence: Round 5 maker’s revised metadata scope names “suggested title,” “description,” and “site icon,” but no preview image. Client calls the automatic lookup “right” without mentioning that omission.
decisions.note: Revised prototype review: the metadata implementation remained incomplete because preview-image collection was still absent.

decisions.evidence: Round 5 maker: “the suggested title remains editable.” Client: “I can still change the title if I like.”
decisions.note: Prototype review: editing the collected title before saving conforms.

decisions.evidence: Round 5 maker: description “isn’t directly editable in this save box.” Client explicitly accepts: “I don’t need to hand-edit those in this box.”
decisions.note: Prototype review: the client expressly accepted departure from the requirement to edit the collected description before saving.

decisions.evidence: Round 6 maker presents keeping the count at one and highlighting the existing bookmark with its title ready to edit. Client: “It didn’t make a second copy… pointed me right to… the one I’d already saved.”
decisions.note: Revised prototype review: an exact duplicate now converges to editing the existing bookmark.

decisions.evidence: Round 7 maker presents a list; the client describes each item as showing “its name, the short description, the site icon, and the address,” but tags are absent and the client says, “This is what I want.”
decisions.note: Prototype review: the presented item display omitted required tags, and the approval did not express that difference.

decisions.evidence: Round 7 maker asks the client to click “Example Domain” to open the saved page. Client: “Clicking the title takes me straight to the page.”
decisions.note: Prototype review: selecting the bookmark title navigates to the original URL; opening a new tab is a compatible implementation choice.

decisions.evidence: Round 8 maker presents immediate removal with count update. Client selects removal from the item menu and describes it as “getting rid of something for good.”
decisions.note: Prototype review: the item can be permanently removed; menu placement is orthogonal to the requirement.

decisions.evidence: Round 9 maker explicitly limits search to “the title, description, and address together.” Client approves those fields, but neither presentation nor response includes bookmark notes.
decisions.note: Prototype review: the enumerated full-text search scope omitted the required note field.

decisions.evidence: Round 9 client asks whether capitalized “Recipe” will match; Round 10 maker demonstrates that it still finds Serious Eats, and the client confirms capitalization does not matter.
decisions.note: Prototype review: the pending case-sensitivity clarification was resolved with conforming case-insensitive search and is counted once.

decisions.evidence: Round 11 maker offers one-collection-per-bookmark versus several tags. Client selects tags because “a single link might be both ‘work’ and ‘reading’” and rejects having to choose one folder.
decisions.note: Prototype review: the alternatives differed in support for many-to-many tagging, and the client selected the reference-conforming alternative.

decisions.evidence: Round 11 maker says overlapping labels are visible on sample items; the client selects the tag arrangement with several labels on one link.
decisions.note: Revised prototype review: tags are now exposed on bookmark items, completing the previously omitted list field.

decisions.evidence: Round 12 maker asks the client to add both “work” and “reading” and states that existing tags can be reused and new tags created while saving. Client chooses the removable-chip interaction.
decisions.note: Prototype review: assigning multiple existing or new tags conforms.

decisions.evidence: Round 12 typing-based tag entry lacks suggestions. Client requests: “As I start typing, if I’ve used a label before, it should suggest it so I can pick the existing one.”
decisions.note: Prototype review: the client requested the missing existing-tag autocomplete behavior.

decisions.evidence: Round 13 maker presents typing “read” and selecting suggested “reading.” Client confirms it offered the existing label and created a removable chip.
decisions.note: Revised prototype review: existing tags are offered during entry as required.

decisions.evidence: Rounds 15–16 maker presents immediate removal followed by an eight-second Undo window. Client selects it while describing Undo as a temporary safety net.
decisions.note: Edge-case review: the grace-period Undo is compatible with an eventual permanent delete and does not replace deletion with archival.

decisions.evidence: Round 17 maker presents blocking “not a link,” leaving the count unchanged, and showing a correction. Client agrees invalid input should not be saved.
decisions.note: Edge-case review: enforcing that the required input is a URL conforms.

decisions.evidence: Round 18 maker offers continuing to save versus retrying when metadata cannot be retrieved. Client selects continue-saving: “Being blocked from saving a perfectly good link would be the real problem.”
decisions.note: Edge-case review: the alternatives differed in whether a valid URL could still be saved, and the client selected the reference-conforming outcome.

decisions.evidence: Round 21 maker presents adding “reading” and then “READING” while retaining one lowercase chip. Client confirms they should not become separate labels.
decisions.note: Edge-case review: preventing duplicate tag names is consistent with tag-name uniqueness.

decisions.evidence: Round 22 maker presents saving `https://example.com/#about` while retaining one bookmark and focusing the existing item. Client agrees that the section fragment should not create another copy.
decisions.note: Edge-case review: compatible URL canonicalization preserves the required convergence to the existing bookmark.

decisions.evidence: Round 23 maker removes the only bookmark, shows the empty collection, and restores it through Undo. Client confirms the removal and restoration behavior.
decisions.note: Edge-case review: deletion continues to work for the last item; the temporary recovery behavior is an additional safeguard.

decisions.evidence: Round 11 maker has the client select “Recipes.” At Round 24 the client clarifies that clicking a label must narrow the collection; Round 25 maker explicitly confirms this is implemented, and the client accepts it.
decisions.note: Prototype-to-implementation review: the carry-forward clarification was resolved by explicit confirmation of tag filtering, so it is one conforming decision rather than a separate unresolved case.

decisions.evidence: After accepting the completed first version in Round 25, the client explicitly identifies “marking links to read later” as an idea “for another time, not anything to hold this up.”
decisions.note: Implementation review: the client surfaced the absent read-later marking requirement and explicitly accepted deferring it.

decisions.evidence: After accepting the completed first version in Round 25, the client identifies “tidying old ones away” as a future idea and says it is “not anything to hold this up.”
decisions.note: Implementation review: in context this surfaces archival as absent and explicitly accepts its deferral; no broader archive-view or reversibility behavior was expressed.
